ii Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders

Message
India's rich heritage of traditional healthcare systems has long provided holistic, time-tested
solutions for the prevention, management, and promotion of health. In recent years, there has been growing
recognition of the significant role that Ayush systems can play in addressing the increasing burden of skin
diseases through patient-centric, and integrative healthcare approaches.
The release of the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) for Dermatological Disorders in the
respective Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Homeopathy (ASUH) systems, with the inclusion of Yoga, marks
another important milestone in our collective efforts to strengthen the integration of Ayush systems into the
national healthcare framework. Building upon the success of the previously released STGs, these
guidelines reaffirm our commitment to harmonizing the wisdom of traditional medicine with contemporary
scientific evidence, thereby enhancing the quality, safety, and accessibility of healthcare services.
These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the prevention, diagnosis, and
management of common dermatological disorders, including Psoriasis, Dermatitis, Vitiligo, Urticaria, and
Dermatophytosis. By offering standardized and system-specific clinical guidance, they will support
healthcare practitioners in delivering safe, effective, and holistic patient care while promoting rational and
evidence-informed clinical practice.
I am confident that these STGs will contribute significantly to improving clinical outcomes,
encouraging integrative models of healthcare, and strengthening the role of Ayush systems in Public health
sector. They will also serve as valuable reference documents for clinicians, academicians, researchers, and
policymakers, fostering greater uniformity and excellence in patient care across the country.
I wholeheartedly appreciate the dedicated efforts of Ayush Vertical under DGHS as well as all the
experts, institutions, researchers, and stakeholders whose invaluable contributions have made the
development of these comprehensive guidelines possible. I am confident that this initiative will further
strengthen the vision of accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare for all through the Ayush systems of
medicine.
(Prataprao Jadhav)

New Delhi

FOREWORD
The standardization of clinical practice is fundamental to ensuring quality, safety, and consistency across
healthcare delivery systems. Recognizing this imperative, the Ayush Vertical, under the leadership and
guidance of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), initiated the systematic development of
Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) for common clinical conditions across traditional systems of
medicine. Building upon the successful publication of our earlier volumes on Musculoskeletal and
Metabolic Disorders, I am pleased to present the third set in the series: Standard Treatment Guidelines
for Dermatological Disorders.
This volume addresses five commonly encountered clinical entities—Psoriasis, Dermatitis, Vitiligo,
Urticaria, and Dermatophytosis. These guidelines are designed to assist Ayush practitioners in delivering
standardized, evidence-informed, and safe clinical care while preserving the foundational diagnostic and
therapeutic principles of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Homeopathy. Beyond routine clinical application,
this document aims to foster consistency in practice, enhance quality assurance, support capacity
building, and provide a framework for future epidemiological and clinical research.
The preparation of these guidelines underscores the steadfast commitment of the Ayush Vertical to
institutionalizing quality assurance within public health services. Developed through an extensive
collaborative mechanism, this document brings together technical expertise from the Ayush Research
Councils, senior academic specialists across all four traditional streams, and distinguished experts from
modern medical specialties. This interdisciplinary approach ensures that the protocols remain deeply
rooted in classical wisdom, scientifically robust, and aligned with modern public health standards.
A defining strength of this publication is its rigorous, field-level validation. To ensure operational
feasibility in real-world clinical environments, the Ayush Vertical, in active collaboration with the
Directorate of Ayush, Government of NCT of Delhi, conducted comprehensive field testing of the draft
protocols. Medical Officers engaged in primary and secondary healthcare delivery tested the guidelines
in their daily practice, providing critical operational feedback. Inclusion of their observations in the final
publication has significantly enhanced its clinical relevance and practical utility.
I place on record my sincere gratitude to the members of the National Expert Committee, the Editorial
Board, subject experts from the Ayush Research Councils, modern medicine specialists, the Directorate
of Ayush (NCT of Delhi), and all participating Medical Officers. Their technical rigor, dedication, and spirit
of collaboration have been crucial in bringing this project to fruition.
I am confident that the Standard Treatment Guidelines for Dermatological Disorders will serve as an
authoritative reference for clinicians, academic faculties, researchers, and public health administrators.
It is our earnest hope that this effort will further strengthen the delivery of accessible, safe, and quality-
driven Ayush healthcare services to the nation.

CASE DEFINITION
Dermatitis refers to inflammation of the skin resulting in erythema, itching, edema, and
vesiculation, often followed by crusting and scaling. It includes a broad spectrum of disorders
such as atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis (irritant/allergic), seborrheic dermatitis, nummular
dermatitis and dyshidrotic dermatitis.1,2
Vicharchika is one among the eighteen types of integumentary diseases enlisted in the
classical textbooks of Ayurveda. It is classified as a Ksudra Kustha, ie minor skin disease. This
skin disorder is characterized by mild to intense itching, papular eruptions, blackish/greyish
discoloration and excessive discharge with the predominant involvement of Kapha Dosha in
general.3,4
INTRODUCTION (Incidence/Prevalence, Morbidity/Mortality/Risk Factors)1,25,6,7,8,9,10,11,12
• Atopic dermatitis affects up to 20% of children and around 10% of adults globally, with
increasing prevalence in industrialized nations.
• Contact dermatitis accounts for nearly 70% of occupational skin diseases worldwide.
• Seborrheic dermatitis is estimated to affect 1–5% of the general population but may
exceed 85% in HIV-infected individuals.
• Nummular dermatitis represents approximately 0.2–0.5% of dermatology cases, while
dyshidrotic dermatitis constitutes 5–20% of hand eczema cases globally.
• In India, similar prevalence patterns are observed, with a significant burden of atopic and
contact dermatitis, particularly among industrial workers and urban populations.

• Morbidity includes chronic pruritus, secondary infections, sleep disturbances, and
psychological impact, although mortality is exceedingly rare.
• Key risk factors across these types of dermatitis include genetic predisposition, atopic
background, impaired epidermal barrier, exposure to irritants or allergens, microbial
dysbiosis, emotional stress, and environmental factors.
• Dermatitis may be entirely endogenous (constitutional) or be entirely exogenous (contact).
The latter consists of irritant and allergic contact reactions. Commonly, dermatitis
has a multifactorial aetiology and may be aggravated by the presence of pathogens
(staphylococcus aureus). Assessment of the relative importance (contribution) of the
possible factors may be difficult and subjective.
Dermatitis/eczematous conditions can be considered under Vicharchika in Ayurveda.
Vicharchika is a disease caused by the vitiation of tridosha with the predominance of
Vata and Kapha. Acharya Sushruta mentions a Vicharchika type with Pitta dominance
also, where there is minimal discharge, excessive itching and pain, and linear skin-lesions
(अलपस्ािावतकण्डिरत्चिरुजाव्ितरावजमती विचरचचिका वपत्तेन ). As per Kustha Samprapti, the three doshas
provoked by the particular nidanas creates shaithilya of Twak, Rakta, Mamsa and Lasika
Dhatus. Further vitiation of doshas causes accumulation in the Shithila Dhatus resulting in
Dosh Dushya Samoorchana. Based on the level of dosha-dushya involvement, various skin
diseases such as Vicharchika are manifested. Dushivisha as well as Raktadushti may also play
roles in manifestation of Kustha including Vicharchika.

CLINICAL EXAMINATION14
A detailed patient’s history should be taken and focus on the following:
• Onset and distribution of lesions
• Inspection to identify skin rashes, redness, dryness, scaling, crusting, discolouration,
thickening and other signs of irritation.
• The severity of pruritus (e.g., keeping patient awake at night)
• Family and/or personal history of the atopic triad. (Atopic triad refers to the genetic
predisposition to develop allergic conditions such as atopic dermatitis, allergic asthma,
allergic rhinitis and other allergies like conjunctivitis)
• Presence of contact allergens
• The presence of triggers including allergens (e.g., dust mites, animal dander), hot showers/
sweating, soaps, fragrances, food hypersensitivities, and synthetic fabrics such as polyester.
Classic physical examination findings of Atopic Dermatitis (depend on the age group).
• Infants develop oedematous papules and plaques that may have vesicles or crust on the
scalp, face, and extensor extremities.

In Ayurvedic classics, Vicharchika is a skin disorder characterized by Kandu or Atikandu
(itching), Pidika (papular eruptions), Shyava (blackish or greyish discoloration), Bahusrava
(excessive or copious discharge), Lasikadhya (excessive watery discharge), Atiruja (excessive
pain), and Raji (manifestation of linear lesions).
1. सकण्डूठः वप्डका श्ािा बहुस्ािा विचरचचिका||२६|| Cha. Chi. 7/26
2. राज्योऽवतकण्डिरतचिरुजठः सरूक्ा भिव्त गारितेषु विचरचचिका्ाम् ||१३|| Su.Ni. 5/13
3. सकण्डूवपटिका श्ािा लसीकाढ्ा विचरचचिका||१८|| A.H.Ni.14/18
According to Acharya Charaka, Vicharchika is considered to have a predominance of Kapha
Dosha. In general, skin disorders involve all three Doshas—Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. This is also
true for Vicharchika, which has involvement of all three Doshas.
The general features outlined in classical Ayurvedic texts may not be present at every stage of
the disease, as they depend on the involvement of the Doshas and the patient’s condition. Thus,
the symptoms of Vicharchika can be correlated with different types of dermatitis, depending
on their clinical presentation. It is also important to note that not every clinical presentation
will have a specific name, allowing physicians with the flexibility to differentiate and label the
condition as needed. For example, in the case of atopic dermatitis or nummular dermatitis,
the dry stage can be correlated with Vicharchika symptoms such as Kandu (itching), Atikandu
(intense itching), Pidaka (papular eruptions), and Shyava (blackish or greyish discoloration).
During this stage, oozing is typically absent. However, in the wet stage of the same disease,
Lasikadhya (excessive watery discharge) may be present.
Dyshidrotic Eczema (DE) may be correlated with Vicharchika with the involvement of Pitta along
with Vata and Kapha, as it commonly occurs in individuals with hyperhidrosis, and symptoms
such as burning sensation and redness are observed in some cases. The symptoms of Atikandu
(Severe itching), Lasika (fluid-filled vesicles), Pidaka are seen in DE patients. In cases of secondary
infections, symptoms mentioned in the classics such as Atiruja (excessive pain), Atisrava (Pus
discharge) may also be observed. Management for this condition should include Pittahara drugs
in addition to the general treatment of Vicharchika if associated with burning sensation and
hyperhidrosis. Daha, Paka, and Putigandha also indicates involvement of Pitta.
In contact dermatitis, symptoms are similar to Vicharchika like Kandu, Daha, Ruja, Srava, Sphota
etc. In addition to the general line of treatment, Garavisha Chikitsa may also be incorporated

PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT
The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating
treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated co
morbidities. If the patient is already under standard care, the physician may advise to continue
the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can be assessed for the same in the
follow ups for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional
physician.
In Ayurveda, Kustha is an umbrella term for various skin diseases. It results from improper diet
and lifestyle that significantly affect physiological and psychological well-being. The causative
factors hint the involvement of Ama visha, Krimi, Rakta and Manas in addition to the Tridoshas.
All the skin diseases are said to be Tridoshaja and is generally considered as chronic.The
permutations and combinations of Nidana decide the Dhatus and Doshas involved, leading to
specific skin diseases.
Management may include Nidana Parivarjana (avoidance of disease-causing factors),
Samprapti Vighatana (the process of disrupting the pathogenesis (Samprapti) of a disease
to facilitate its treatment and to facilitate non-recurrence) and relevant principles of Krimi,
Visha, Visarpa and Jwara Chikitsa. The clinician should be able to diagnose the doshas and
dooshyas involved and the level of involvement to decide the selection of drugs and duration
of treatment.

These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment for need for management/

• Secondary bacterial or viral infection (pus, fever)

(A) Preventive Treatment
The effective management of Dermatitis (Vicharchika) focuses on both preventive and curative
measures, emphasizing diet, lifestyle and psychological well-being. Preventive measures
involve Nidana Parivarjana, which refers to the avoidance of causative factors of the disease.
Diet
It is recommended that one’s Satmya Ahara (habitually suitable and agreeable food) be taken
warm and fresh, avoiding preparations that are excessively dry or heavy. The food should
be consumed mindfully, with proper chewing and at a steady, moderate pace. The intake of
Viruddhahara (incompatible foods) may contribute to the onset of skin diseases; therefore,
such foods should be avoided.
Life style
Following Dinacharya (daily regimen) and Ritucharya (seasonal regimen) as prescribed in
classical Ayurvedic texts helps in maintaining overall health and preventing diseases
Yoga24
Dermatitis is a multifactorial condition influenced by immune dysregulation and psychosocial
stress, where stress aggravates inflammation, elevates pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-
6, TNF-α), and delays skin healing. From a yogic standpoint, it reflects an imbalance at both
physiological and psychological levels. Yoga offers a holistic, evidence-based approach by
reducing stress and modulating neuroendocrine function through practices like Dhyana and
Yoga Nidra, which help lower cortisol levels. Pranayama techniques such as Nadi Shodhana
and Bhramari improve autonomic balance and reduce systemic inflammation. Additionally,

Asanas like Tadasana, Trikonasana, Padahastasna, Ardachakrasana, Bhujangasana, Setu
Bandhasana enhance circulation and support skin repair. Collectively, yoga exerts anti-
inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, while improving psychological well-being and
quality of life. (Proper guidance from a yoga expert is essential before practicing yoga for skin
disorders)

Atopic Dermatitis:
Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common inflammatory skin condition occurring in both pediatric
and adult patients. Pruritus is a clinical hallmark of the disease, and patients with AD often
experience disruptions to their quality of life. Clinically, AD is characterized by pruritus,
eczematous skin changes, and age-specific lesion distribution patterns. Infants and young
children tend to have AD lesions on their face and extensor surfaces of their extremities while
older children and adults tend to have AD lesions on flexural surfaces of their extremities.
Many patients also experience a chronic and relapsing disease course. Due to the chronicity
and severe pruritus, lesions often undergo secondary changes like lichenification. Patients
with AD can experience a number of comorbidities including other atopic disease (i.e. allergic
rhinitis, asthma), skin infections, cardiovascular, and neuropsychiatric illnesses.

Nummular Dermatitis:
Nummular eczema is characterized by sharply defined, oval or coin-shaped, erythematous,
eczematous plaques. Typically, the size of the lesion varies from 1 to 10cm in diameter. The
lesions are usually multiple and symmetrically distributed. Sites of predilection include the
lower limbs followed by the upper limbs. The lesions are usually intensely pruritic. The
diagnosis is mainly clinical based on the characteristic round to oval erythematous plaques
in a patient with diffusely dry skin. Nummular eczema should be distinguished from other
annular lesions.

Dyshidrotic Eczema:
Dyshidrotic eczema (DE) or acute palmoplantar eczema is a common cause of hand dermatitis
in adults. It is a vesiculobullous disorder of the hands and soles. It is an intraepidermal
spongiosis of the thick epidermis in which accumulation of edema causes the formation of
small, tense, clear, fluid-filled vesicles on the lateral aspects of the fingers that can become
large and form bullae.

Contact Eczema:
Contact dermatitis (CD) is an inflammatory skin condition triggered by chemicals or metal ions
that cause irritant effects, or by contact allergens that modify proteins and induce immune
responses, primarily through T cells. CD can manifest as irritant contact dermatitis or allergic
contact dermatitis, both of which can be acute or chronic.
Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct chemical damage and does not involve immune
reactions or prior sensitization, leading to similar responses among most individuals exposed
to irritants.
In contrast, allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction (type IV) that
requires prior exposure to allergens. Skin lesions from CD can occur due to various irritants
or allergens, UV radiation, microbial exposure, or intrinsic factors. When related to work
environments, it may be classified as occupational contact dermatitis, often due to substances
like alcohol-based disinfectants, detergents, or latex gloves. Parthenium dermatitis is a form
of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) caused by airborne particles (especially sesquiterpene
lactones) from the weed Parthenium hysterophorus, leading to itchy rashes (papules/plaques)
on exposed skin (face, neck, chest, limbs).

General Instructions
• Keep skin dry and clean, especially in areas like skin folds, armpits, and groin areas.
Hand Hygiene:
• Washing hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching potentially
contaminated surfaces or individuals.
• Don’t share towels, clothing, razors, and personal care items.
Foot Hygiene:
• Wear breathable shoes and moisture-wicking socks, especially in wlarm or humid
weather.
• Dry feet thoroughly, particularly between the toes, after showering or swimming.
• Avoid Walking Barefoot in Public Areas:
Clothing Choices:
• Opt for loose-fitting, breathable clothing made of natural fibers like cotton, which can
help prevent moisture buildup.
• Allow shoes to dry out completely between uses to prevent fungal growth.

Nail Hygiene:
• Keep nails short and clean, and avoid biting or scratching the skin, especially if you
have an existing fungal infection.
Hygiene in Communal Areas:
• Wash exercise clothes after each use.

Referral Criteria
• Lack of clinical improvement after 4-6 weeks of individualized treatment
• Extensive skin involvement (>30% BSA), especially in children or elderly.
• Severe pruritus leading to sleep disturbance or psychological distress.
• Severe pain with burning or stinging sensation.
• Secondary infection suspected due to oozing, crusting, fever, or lymphadenopathy.
• Diagnostic uncertainty (e.g., differential diagnosis from psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis,
scabies).
• Evidence of an increase in severity/complications.
• Coexisting systemic diseases (diabetes, hypothyroidism, renal impairment) affecting skin
healing.
• Recurrent relapses despite compliance with therapy.
• Suspected allergic etiology needing patch testing or further evaluation.
• Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living

CASE DEFINITION
Superficial infection caused by a dermatophyte is known as Dermatophytosis or ringworm
infection. This term is a misnomer because worms are not involved1. “Tinea”, the Latin name
for worm, describes the serpentine appearance of the skin lesions2.
As per Ayurveda, Dadru is characterised by Kanduh [associated with itching sensation],
Ragah [reddish nodules], Tamra VarnaPidka [copper coloured papule/eruptions], Udgata
Mandalam/UtsannaMandalata [elevated ring-shaped plaque], Dirgha Pratana [spreading
out], Durvavat[resembling Durva], Atasi Kusuma Chhavi [resembling the flower of Atasi],
Anushangi [chronic /associated over a long period]3
INTRODUCTION (incidence/prevalence /morbidity/mortality/risk factors)
• Dermatophytes (keratinophilic fungi) are the most common cutaneous fungal infections
seen in humans affecting skin, hairs and nails with a considerable morbidity.4
• According to World Health Organization (WHO), the prevalence rate of superficial mycotic
infection worldwide has been found to be 20-25%.
• Its prevalence varies in different countries. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical
countries like India where the heat and humidity are high for most part of the year.5,6
Community - based surveys and dermatology outpatient data show 20-30% prevalence,
especially in humid regions. In some areas, up to 50-60% of dermatology OPD cases are
due to dermatophytosis.
• An epidemic of recalcitrant dermatophyte infection has engulfed India and many part of the
world and the species that is dominant has been controversially named as Trichophyton
indotinae7. This is resistant to many front-line drugs. This has led to an alteration in the
immunity8. A National Task force was formed which details the cause of recalcitrant
infection as below. Notably steroid abuse has lead to varied forms of Tinea classically
tinea incognito and majocchi variant which do not respond to conventional agents.

• The new species Trichophyton Indotinea has unique mechanisms of resistance and is fast
becoming the most dominant variety of dermatophytosis in India.
• Chronic and recurrent cases have increased significantly in the last 5-10 years due to
overuse of topical steroids and antifungal creams which have made them resistant to
common antifungal drugs.
• Dermatophytosis is not life threatening, but it causes severe itching and discomfort,
social embarrassment and stigma, sleep disturbances, work absenteeism and reduced
productivity.
• Study using DLQI (Dermatology Life Quality Index) shows moderate to severe impact on
quality of life in 40-60% of chronic/ recurrent cases. Psychological stress, anxiety and low
self-esteem are common.10,11
All skin diseases in Ayurveda have been classified under the broad heading of “Kustha”
which are further categorized in to Mahakustha &Kshudrakustha12. As per Acharyas, Dadru
is a skin disease which is characterized by circular erythematous patches (Mandala), itching
(Kandu), burning sensation (Daha), redness (Raga), and eruption of elevated lesions (Utsanna
Mandala)- which mirror the clinical features of Tinea corporis and cruris. The Sthana (site of
occurrence) of the Dadrukustha is fourth layer of skin and the doshic predominance is kapha
pitta.13 Acharya Charaka included Dadru among kshudrakustha while Acharya Susrutha has
classified Dadru among Mahakusthas, Acharya Vagbhata highlighted the Anushangi nature
of Dadrukustha and the spread resembling Durva grass. The symptoms of Daha (Burning
sensation) and Srava (discharge) are also associated symptoms of the disease.
CLINICAL PRESENTATION 14,15,16
Typical Lesion-
• A typical lesion of dermatophytosis is an annular or arcuate plaque which spreads
centrifugally (away from the centre).
• The edge is active, showing papulo-vesiculation, pustulation and scaling, while the centre
is usually relatively clear.
• In chronic lesion there may be nodules, hyperpigmentation and even lichenification
(thickening, hyperpigmentation and increased skin markings) in the centre.
• In India due to steroid abuse altered morphologies including Tinea incognito and Majocchi
Granuloma are seen . Fig 1

Dadru typically presents with red, circular patches on the skin that are raised and itchy. The
main symptoms include intense itching (kandu), reddish discoloration (raga), small eruptions
or papules (pidaka), and ring-shaped raised lesions (utsanna mandala Pari Mandala). These
lesions often spread gradually and may resemble the Flax flower (Atasi Pushpa) or Bermuda
Grass (Durva). In some cases, burning sensation, scaling, or oozing can occur.17,18
According to Dalhaṇa, Dadru is of two types: Sita (white), Asita (black)19. Asita Dadru is
considered difficult to treat due to its severity, deep tissue involvement, and chronic nature. In
contrast, Sita Dadru is easily curable, superficial, and causes milder symptoms. Dadru Kushtha
rarely has complications; improper treatment can lead to further Dosha Dushti (vitiation of
Dosha), causing increased Dhatu involvement and chronicity. Dadru Kushtha generally has
good prognosis.
CLINICAL EXAMINATION11
A thorough clinical examination helps to diagnose, classify and differentiate from other
dermatoses.
General Inspection
It includes observation of site(s) of infection, number, size and distribution of lesion. Common
sites include groin, axillae, trunk, face, feet, hands, nails, scalp. Ask about onset, progression,
recurrence, family history and steroid/ antifungal use.

Evaluation and Assessment
The Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI is a practical 10-question tool assessing the
impact of skin disease on patients’ lives, scored from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating
greater impairment.26
The Dermatology-specific Quality of Life (DSQL) instrument measures physical,
psychological, and social limitations through 36 items, focusing on disease-specific impacts.27
Skindex-16 is a validated 16-item questionnaire scored on a 0–6 Likert scale, evaluating the
effects of skin diseases on quality of life, with lower scores indicating better QoL28.

Red Flag signs
These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment-
• Secondary bacterial infection.
• Intractable alopecia cases causing permanent hair loss in tinea capitis
• Uncontrolled Diabetes-mellitus
• Lower extremity cellulitis in cases of tinea pedis.
• Underlying severe immunodeficiency due to HIV/AIDS.
• Severe wide spread infection causing significant pain or inflammation or eczematization
irrespective of treatment.
(A) Prevention Management:
Avoidance of the etiological factors mentioned in Kustharoga nidana(food, dietary habits,
lifestyle and behavioural characters) is the most important preventive measure.
Other preventive measures:
• Following Dinacharya, Ritucharya, and Sadvritta.
Yoga
Yoga practice plays a supportive role by:
• Boosting immunity
• Reducing stress. (which can worsen fungal infection)
• Enhancing blood circulation to the skin.
• Supportive detoxification and hormonal balance.
Yoga can play a supportive role in prevention by enhancing overall immunity and promoting
skin health. Regular practice of asanas like Shavasana, Padmasana, Sidhasana, Makarasana,
and Suryanamaskara improves blood circulation and detoxification, helping to maintain
healthy skin. Pranayama and meditation reduce stress, which is known to lower immunity
and increase susceptibility to infections. Shat kriya and yoga nidra helps in deep relaxation for
immune system repair.

General Instructions
• Keep skin dry and clean, especially in areas like skin folds, armpits, and groin areas.
Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders 47

Hand Hygiene:
• Washing hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching potentially
contaminated surfaces or individuals.
• Don’t Share towels, clothing, razors, and personal care items.
Foot Hygiene:
• Wear breathable shoes and moisture-wicking socks, especially in warm or humid weather.
• Dry feet thoroughly, particularly between the toes, after showering or swimming.
• Avoid Walking Barefoot in Public Areas:
Clothing Choices:
• Opt for loose-fitting, breathable clothing made of natural fibers like cotton, which can help
prevent moisture buildup.
• Allow shoes to dry out completely between uses to prevent fungal growth.
Nail Hygiene:
• Keep nails short and clean, and avoid biting or scratching the skin, especially if you have
an existing fungal infection.
Hygiene in Communal Areas:
• Wash Exercise Clothes After Each Use.
*These are general pathya-apathya guidelines to be followed in skin diseases. However, they
may be tailored on a case-to-case basis, taking into account the patient’s prakriti, type of
Kustha, seasonal variations, and other relevant factors.
Follow Up: Once in every 15 days or as needed, for effective management of the condition.
Referral Criteria
• No response at all after 2-3 weeks of treatment period.
• Uncontrolled comorbidities like diabetes mellitus, hypertension etc.
• Evidence of an increase in severity/complications
• Diagnostic uncertainty.
• Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living.
At Level 2: (CHC/ Small hospitals 10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such as routine,
investigation, X-ray)
Clinical Diagnosis: Same as level 1. The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be
evaluated thoroughly for any complications.
Investigations: The diagnosis would be primarily clinical. However, some investigations may
be necessary to investigate complications or exclude other differential diagnoses as follows:
• Renal function test.
• Fasting lipids, glucose, and thyroid functions.
Management: If there is Bahudoshatwa, the patient may be admitted to a Level 2 facility for
Snehapana, Shodhana, Rakta Mokshana, with constant monitoring and observation.

CASE DEFINITION 1, 2
Psoriasis is a common, chronic, inflammatory and proliferative condition of the skin and may
be associated with systemic manifestations in many organ systems. The most characteristic
lesions are red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, particularly over the extensor
surfaces and scalp. It can cause itching, irritation, burning and stinging, and the extent and
severity vary enormously over time and between individuals.

INTRODUCTION (incidence/ prevalence, morbidity/mortality/ risk factors) 1, 3-9]
• Psoriasis vulgaris is a chronic, non-communicable, disfiguring, and disabling disease with
negative impact of varied degree on a patient’s quality of life (QoL).
• It affects males and females equally. About 2–3% of the population have psoriasis and
10% of these individuals will develop psoriatic arthritis. Of this group, in 3–5% of them,
it is severe 5
58 Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders

• According to the World Health Organization, approximately 0.09% - 11.43% (incidence,
46,22,594, prevalence 4,08,05,386) of the global population suffers from psoriasis.
• In India, the prevalence of this illness varies from 0.44 to 2.8%; both sexes affected equally
with few studies showing male predominance and most of the patients are in their third or
fourth decade at the time of presentation.
• The lifetime risk of developing the disease is strongly associated with a family history; if
no parent has psoriasis, the risk is 4%; if one parent has psoriasis, the risk is 14-28% and
if both parents have psoriasis, the risk is 40-65%.
PATHOGENESIS AND ITS THERAPUETIC IMPLICTIONS5
1. Genetics:
There are two peaks of onset of psoriasis (Fig.). Type I has onset in the second and third
decades and a more common family history of psoriasis. Type II has onset in late adulthood
in patients without obvious family history.
2. Hyperproliferation
The growth fraction of the upper layer of skin known as the epidermis is increased with the
basal cell being increased 7x compared with normal skin. The cell turnover time decreases
from 30 to 5 days, similarly the cell cycle time reduces from 311 to 36 hours.
3. Inflammation
Psoriasis is now known to be a autoimmune disorder with CD4T cells, Th17 and Th 12
cells playing an important role.8 Notably these cells are determined by cytokines that
are the target of novel drugs known as biologic which have changed the therapeutic of
psoriasis.9 [fig] Psoriatic keratinocytes contain high levels of antimicrobial peptides which
may account for the surprisingly low incidence of bacterial skin infection.
4. Psoriasis is also now appreciated to be an intimate part of the metabolic syndrome,
associated with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease.
Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders 59

Fig - A depiction of the major T cell subtypes and cytokines that determine Psoriasis. Drugs
that inhibit these cytokines are available and are known as Biologics
In Ayurveda, psoriasis corresponds broadly to Kustha, a term for chronic skin diseases caused
by dosha-dhatu-mala imbalances and systemic disturbances [10]. Psoriasis aligns with subtypes
such as EkaKustha, Kitibha, Sidhma, Vipadika, Mandala, pundarika and Carmadala, involving
predominance of Vata-Kapha in plaque types, Pitta-Kapha in pustular forms, and Vata-Pitta
in psoriatic arthritis [11]. The pathogenesis (Samprapti) includes dietary and lifestyle factors
causing impaired digestion (Agni), accumulation of toxins (Ama), and obstruction of channels
(Srotorodha), paralleling immune dysregulation and systemic inflammation [12].
Ayurveda also recognizes the systemic nature of psoriasis through its holistic view of Kustha,
linking it to chronic metabolic and psychological imbalances. Comorbidities like cardiovascular
disorders, metabolic syndrome, and depression are conceptualized as manifestations of
Dushivisha (chronic toxins), Mandagni (impaired digestive fire), and Avarana Vata (obstruction
in channels), emphasizing the need for comprehensive management addressing physical and
mental health [13,14].This integrated understanding supports the use of Shodhana (detoxification),
Shamana (palliative treatment), Rasayana (rejuvenation), and Satvavajaya (psychological
therapies) to address both cutaneous lesions and systemic complications effectively [15].

CLINICAL EXAMINATION21
Psoriasis is mostly diagnosed on the basis of clinical examination of the skin, scalp,and
nails along with review of patients smoking history, medical history and family history. The
characteristic skin lesions are sharply demarcated, scaly, erythematous raised plaques, either
painful or itching red patches covered with silvery scales. The lesions vary in shape and may be
ovoid, round, or irregular and are often symmetrically distributed. Common areas of involvement
include extensor surface of body, elbows, knees, scalp, trunk, lumbosacral region and nails. A
skin biopsy needed in some cases to confirm the diagnosis and to rule out other diseases.
Ayurveda clinical examination comprises of darshana, sparshana and prashna pareeksha
which provides leads to dosha predominance of clinical manifestation of psoriasis.
Dashavidha Pareeksha (Tenfold examination) are also included in Ayurveda clinical
examination to formulate adequate treatment protocol.

1) Bedside tests Two simple bedside tests were done to confirm the diagnosis.
a) Grattage test This is positive when scales are accentuated by grating lesions with a glass

2) Skin biopsy Skin biopsy (done in doubtful cases) shows epidermis and dermal changes.

acanthosis, suprapapillary thinning, elongation of rete ridges and collection
of neutrophils in the epidermis (spongiform pustule of Kogoj and Munro’s
microabscess). Dermal changes: dilatation and tortuosity of capillary loops in
dermal papillae, and lymphocyte infiltrates in the upper dermis.

Classification of severity and prognostic assessment
• Psoriasis area severity index (PASI) score [26]
The PASI is a widely used instrument in psoriasis trials that assesses and grades the
severity of psoriatic lesions and the patient›s response to treatment. It produces a numeric
score ranging from 0 to 72. A 75% reduction in the PASI score (PASI 75) is the current
benchmark for most clinical trials in psoriasis.
• Nail psoriasis Severity index. [27]
This scale is used to evaluate the severity of nail bed psoriasis and nail matrix psoriasis
by area of involvement in the nail unit. The NAPSI will be useful during clinical trials for
evaluating response to treatment of psoriatic nails.
PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT:
The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating
treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated co-
morbidities. If the patient is already under standard conventional care, the physician may
advice to continue the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can assess/consider
for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional physician in
the follow ups. Must check about the intake of drugs that can trigger or exaggerate psoriasis
in the history of the patient.
According to Ayurveda, Kustha is a disease that arises due to improper diet and lifestyle
(mithya ahara and vihara)[28], along with certain causative factors (nidana) that also impact
psychological aspects. So, in the management of psoriasis, both prevention and curative
aspects concentrate on diet, life style and psychological component.

Red Flags
These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment for need for management
through modern medicine.
• Patients with generalized pustular psoriasis or erythrodermic psoriasis with high grade
fever.
• Psoriatic arthritis significantly impacting a person’s physical, psychological or social well-
being.
• Psoriasis with co morbid disorders
(A) Prevention Management
Diet
Ayurveda dietary directives termed as Aṣṭāhāra-vidhi-viśeṣa [29] principles are essential in diet
planning for prevention of psoriasis for high-risk group patients. It is also advised that one’s
satmya ahara (habitual, agreeable food) be served warm, fresh, neither overly dry nor heavy,
and consumed mindfully with thorough chewing at a measured pace.
Life style
Ayurveda emphasizes adherence to dinacharya (daily routine) and ritucharya (seasonal
routine), with particular attention to following dinacharya in the correct sequence.
Yoga
Various yoga practices may be helpful in the management of psoriasis, such as Shavasana
(Corpse Pose), Bhujangasana (Cobra pose), Setu Bandhasana (Bridge Pose), Trikonasana
(Triangle Pose), Balasana (Child’s Pose). Certain Pranayam and meditation techniques like
Anulom Vilom (Alternate Nostril Breathing), Bhramari (Humming Bee Breath), and Kapalbhati
(Skull Shining Breath) will also help in reducing anxiety, emotional stress, cellular healing,
reducing stress-related inflammation and promoting a positive mental state.
(B) Curative management:

According to Ayurvedic principles, the treatment of psoriasis primarily depends on identifying
the predominant vitiated dosha, as reflected by its clinical manifestations.
Shodhana:
As per Ayurveda classical literature, Shodhana chikitsa is indicated in bahudosha [33.
The ‘Shodhana’ will be followed by rasayana protocol which aims at stabilizing dhathu which
helps to prevent recurrence.
Shamana:
Shamana therapy is primarily indicated in conditions with madhya (moderate) or alpa (mild)
dosha dushti. Assessment of bahu, madhyama, and alpa doṣa can be integrated with
objective parameters-for example, the PASI (area and erythema–induration–desquamation

scores), overall severity of clinical features, and the vulnerability/functional significance of the
involved sites (e.g., face, genitals, palms/soles, nail unit, flexures).
Shamana therapy involves both internal and external formulations, such as kwatha, arishta,
churna, ghrita, taila, and lepa.
In psoriasis, bahirparimarjana chikitsa (external therapy) is particularly beneficial when the
vitiated doshas are cleared at the level of deeper dhathus and get localized at the level of
the twak (skin)[34]. In cases of bahu dosha avastha (excessive dosha aggravation), Shamana
chikitsa is administered after Shodhana therapy, to pacify the remaining doshas.
Satvavajayam:
Satvavajaya chikitsa or psychotherapy in Ayurveda is indicated through dhee, dhairya and
atmaadi vijnaanam. This has a major role in correcting psoriatic complications including
psoriatic depression.

B. INTERVENTIONS
At Level 1: Solo physician clinic/health clinic/PHC (Optimal standard of treatment where
technology and resources are limited).
Psoriasis cases with mild to moderate severity, BSA<10 can be treated in level 1. BSA>10,
non-responding cases of mild to moderate severity and severe cases shall be referred to level
2 and 3. The varieties of psoriasis like guttate, erythrodermic psoriasis, generalized pustular
psoriasis, psoriasis with co-morbidities, associated depression, cardiometabolic risks may also
be referred to level 2 and 3.
Fastly spreading psoriasis with acuteness of symptoms as in visarpa, where continuous
monitoring is needed shall be referred to level 2 and 3. Psoriasis with bahu doshavastha with
recurrences and relapses shall be also referred to level 2 and 3.
Clinical diagnosis: Psoriasis is entirely diagnosed clinically with thorough medical history
and physical examination, including BMI. However, some investigations, such as complete
hemogram, urine routine/microscopic, C-reactive protein, fasting blood sugar, postprandial
blood sugar levels, and serum uric acid levels can be advised.
Management:
Prevention protocol:
Diet: Ayurveda based dietary advisories for prevention of skin disease can be followed as part
of primary prevention.
Lifestyle: Life style advocacies based on Ayurveda sleep regimen, vegadharana, promotion
of vyayama, following proper dinacharya with udwarthana therapy (powder massage) and
rithucharya to prevent seasonal exacerbations.
Curative Intervention:
At level 1, curative intervention is solely based on Shamana protocol based on dosha
predominance of clinical manifestation.
Plaque psoriasis –Vata kapha Kustha (charma Kustha, eka Kustha, kitibha)-
• In active phase( pro-inflammatory phase),Manjishtadi kwatha ,Punarnavadi kwatha,,Vilwadi
gutika,Dooshivishari gutika, Arogya vardhini gutika,Avipatti churna,Nishunti shadanga
(Shadanga excluding sunthi) ,Chandrakala Rasa etc can be advocated.
• Mahamanjishtadi kwatha and Patolakaturohinyadi kwatha can be given in the sub acute
phase.
• Ayyappala kera taila, Dinesavalyadi kera oil, Jeevanthyadi yamaka, Vajraka ghrtha and
Mahātikta Ghṛta can be advocated as Shamana medicine in vatakapha phase.
• The external applications shall be withheld in the pittanubandha conditions as in acute
phase and shall be only applied after inflammation has been subsided.

Treatment principle of vipadika can be adopted. In exudative and bleeding phase, the medicines
mentioned in acute phase of vata kapha Kustha can be used. In dry vata kapha phases, non-
exudative non-painful presentation, medicines mentioned in sub-acute/chronic phases can
be advocated. The external applications in subacute and chronic phases include jeevanthyadi
yamaka and mahathiktaka ghrita lepa.
Scalp psoriasis:
The treatment principle is similar to plaque psoriasis. External scalp applications include
Ayyappala kera taila and durvadi taila.
Psoriatic arthritis (Vatarakta):
It is seen associated in 30% of psoriasis cases. The treatment principle includes the treatment
protocol of plaque psoriasis and vatarakta treatment protocol including Mahamanjishtadi
kwatha, shaddharanam churna/tablet and Simhanada guggulu for arthritic management.
Manibhadra gula can be used internally in all varieties of psoriasis when active inflammatory

Referral Criteria
• A PASI score of 5 to 10 is considered moderate disease, and a score more than 10 is
considered severe with substantial impact of quality of life and daily living.
• Generalized pustular psoriasis or erythrodermic psoriasis patients can be referred to a

• Uncontrolled co-morbidities

At Level 2: (CHC/ Small hospitals (10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such
as routine investigation, X-ray)
Clinical Diagnosis:
The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be evaluated thoroughly for any
complications. Identification of patient specific etiopathological factors (nidana) in diet and
lifestyle, classification based on dosha involvement and staging of the disease based on dhatu
involvement should be done to plan the treatment accordingly.
Investigations: The diagnosis would be primarily clinical, along with some investigations
which will be necessary to investigate complications or exclude other differential diagnosis
as follows:
• Complete blood count/ ESR
• Renal function Test, liver function test,
• Fasting lipids, glucose, and thyroid functions
• Complete urine examination
• High sensitivity C-reactive protein.
• Serum electrolytes
• X-ray of affected Joints (Psoriatic arthritis)
• Tests for Biologics is referred to a specialized tertiary level center
Management
OPD/IPD level management:
In addition to the management mentioned in Level 1, staging and classification of the psoriasis
based on dhatus affected and doshas involved should be done at level 2 to determine the
prognosis and mode of management.
The sadhya (curable) Kustha roga affecting only rasa, rakta and mamsa can be treated at OPD
level and yapya (managed with strict diet and regimen but not completely curable) Kustha
roga which affects medodhatu should be treated in a hospital with constant follow up to
prevent recurrence.
The cases in which only alpadoshatwa, is present may be treated at the OPD level with
identification of specific nidanas, nidanaparivarjana, vicharanasnehapana, shodhana,
naimittikarasayana and sesha dosha shamana. When the psoriatic lesions are limited to skin,
it can be treated under the line of treatment of Kustha rogas and raktavritavata.
When Shodhana is done, the bala of the patient should be taken into consideration. In vata
predominant conditions, snehapana and anulomana with Kusthaharasnehas are advised and
madhyama and pravarashodhana are avoided. Vamana is indicated in psoriasis with kapha
predominance and those affecting upper parts of the body (example, scalp psoriasis). Virechana
is indicated in pitta predominance and those affecting lower parts of the body (example,
pustular psoriasis, inverse psoriasis). Shardikavirechana can be employed for shodhana of
Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders 79

pitta in September month where predominant pitta vitiation is involved. Vasantika vamana
can be employed for shodhana of kapha in February-March months where aggravation of
kapha is seen.
Madhutailikavasti indicated for Kustha and Prameha can be given in psoriatic arthropathy
which has become chronic and shows signs of vata pitta or vata involvement .Nasya can be
effectively used in psoriasis affecting the scalp. It also reduces anxiety and stress and also
improves sleep.
If there is bahudoshatwa, the patient may be admitted in Level 2 hospital for Achasnehapana,
madhyama to pravarashodhana (vamana and virechana), rasayana, with constant monitoring
and observation. When the joints are involved in psoriatic arthropathy, vatarakta and vatavyadhi
line of treatment are applicable.
• Shodhana (bio-purificatory measures) including both vamana (therapeutic emesis)
and virechana (therapeutic purgation) after snehapana (internal oleation) is the first
line of treatment in psoriasis along with external therapies like Takradhara (streaming
medicated buttermilk over forehead) which has effect on psychosomatic conditions.
Vamana (therapeutic emesis) and virechana (therapeutic purgation) should be followed by
Rasayana chikitsa (rejuvenation therapy) and finally Shamana aushadhas (dosha pacifying
medicines) are indicated for asesha dosha shaman (complete pacification of doshas) .
Snehapana Vamana Snehapana Virechana Rasayana Shamana.
• The treatments like Shodhana and Rasayana indicated in maharogas (severe illnesses)
like Kustha involve IPD management with constant monitoring for any shodhanavyapat
(complications due to bio-purificatory therapies).
• Rasayana chikitsa should be done in all cases for preventing recurrence (apunarbhava)
which is very common in psoriasis due to involvement of autoimmunity (ojovisramsa).
• Asthimajjagata (for example, psoriatic arthropathy) Kustha should be identified and treated
after educating the patient for lifelong diet and lifestyle modifications and treatment with
constant follow-up.
• In cases where complications which need specialty management are present, patients
may be referred to specific departments in level 3.
Shamana chikitsa (dosha pacifying therapy):
The treatment of psoriasis involves both anta: and bahiparimarjana methods with repeated
shodhana and shamana considering its chronic and recurrent nature. The general line of
treatment of Kustha rogas are applicable to all psoriatic types but the medicines or drugs may
be selected according to the dosha involvement in that particular patient and the dhatus and
part of the body affected.69The list of Samanoushadhis that can be used for the management
of psoriasis is given in table No:9
Purification/ other procedures
Shodhana chikitsa (bio-purificatory procedures): A general line of shodhana treatment along
with external therapeutic procedures is given below for psoriasis and psoriatic arthropathy
cases which can be modified according to the dosha involvement and the conditions of the
particular patient.

i. Deepana and pachana- with Shaddharana churna or Hingwashtakachurna70or
Vaishwanarachurna71 or Ajamojadichurna72or Bhaskara lavanachurna73- 3-6 twice daily
before food or Chitrakadi gutika74.for a duration of 3 days or till the patient have good
appetite.
ii. Snehapana- with Panchatiktakaghrita or Aragwadhaghrita or Tiktakaghrita or
Mahatiktakaghrita - starting from 30 ml till samyaksnigdha lakshana (in arohana doses
increased according to agni). Duration of 3 to 7 days. Sadya snehapana is indicated in
children and adolescents.
iii. Abhyanga and Swedana- Eladi kera or Nalpamaraditaila or Nimbaditaila or any
suitable oil as per dosha involvement indicated for Kustha or twakroga followed by
ushnambusnana. Duration of 3 days.
iv. Vamana- with Madanapippali, Nimba, Vacha, Saindhava and Madhu (or) Vacha
Yashtimadhu Madanapippali in Nimba swarasa with honey (or) Any vamana yoga
specifically indicated for skin disease. Duration: One day.
v. Samsarjana krama- Peyadi karma as per avara, madhyama or pravarashuddhi for 3/5/7
days.
vi. Virechana- with Nimbamritadierandataila, Avipattikara churna or Avipatti choorna,
Trivrit choorna or Triphalakwatha or other virechana drugs according to the dosha
predominance. Other internal medicines are stopped during virechana and restarted
during or after samsarjana krama.
vii. Samsarjana krama after virechana as per avara, madhyama or pravarashuddhi for 3/5/7
days. During snehapana, vamana, virechana and samsarjana krama period other internal
medicines are stopped.
viii. Sarvanga Kashaya dhara. With Aragwadhadikashaya or Manjishtadikashaya or
Panchatiktaka Kashaya or any twakdoshahara and raktaprasadana kashaya.
ix. Takradhara- with Musta Amalakitakra or Aragwadhaditakra or Manjishtaditakra or
Panchatiktakatakra for 7 days. Takradhara may be extended to 14 or 21 days as per
dosha status. In children, Shirolepam may be done instead of dhara. When shirolepam is
done, amalaki and buttermilk prepared in kashayasiddha ksheera are used and Talam is
also done with Rasnadi or Kachuradichurna with Dhanvantaram taila75 or Bala taila76or
Nimbamritaditaila.
x. Prachhana/ Raktamokshana/ Siravedha: As per locations of lesions on lalata, hasta
pada or shiras. Prachana is done in alpadosha status. In bahudosha, Siravedha is advised.
Jalooka can be applied in children.
• All internal medicines are continued till dosha and rogashamanaalso considering
upashayaanupashaya.
• Rasayana drugs are started after dosha and rogashamana and continued for a
period of one to 6 months.
• Ayurvediya Swasthavritta is to be followed during treatment and continued after
complete rogashamana.

Referral Criteria
• Same as mentioned earlier at level 1, plus
• Failure of acute exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
• In erythrodermic patients with generalized pustular psoriasis, patients with febrile and
unstable vitals or secondary infections.

At Level 3: Ayush hospitals are attached with teaching institutions, District Level/ Integrated/
State Ayush Hospitals, Tertiary care allopathic hospitals having Ayush facilities, and multiple
departments/ facilities for diagnosis and interventions. Additional facilities like dieticians,
counselling, and physiotherapy must be provided.
Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Levels 1& 2. Confirm diagnosis and severity with the help of
investigations such as skin biopsy (only done for cases in which clinical diagnosis is not clear),
Further investigations like inflammatory bio markers, ECHO, MRI, CT scan, and chemical
analysis of uric acid renal stones, Fibroscan(to detect early liver damage in patients with a
history of methotrexate used for 2-3 years and alcohol consumption) etc may be advised as
per individual case needs.
Management-
The treatment strategy planning at level 3 is also based on dosha dominance and includes
purificatory therapies for bahudosha Kustha, and subsequent rasayana medicines for
strengthening the purified dhathu, as mentioned in Level 2. In the case of madhyama dosha
or alpa dosha Kustha, shamanoushadhi will be utilized as per dosha dominance and dhathu
involvement. The medicines that can be utilized in the treatment of psoriasis is given in Table No:
9. The treatment of psoriasis will not be complete without nidana parivarjana or identification
and avoidance of etiological factors which may vary from individual-to-individual.
Management of psoriatic complications:
• In metabolic complications associated with psoriasis including metabolic syndrome,
NAFLD, anemia and liver cirrhosis, patolamooladi kwatha, patolakaturohinyadi kwatha,
vasa guduchyadi kwatha, arogyavardhini vati can be advocated
• In psychiatric complications associated with psoriasis, the snehana samanoushadha
including kalyanaka ghrita, maha kalyanaka ghrita; manasa mitravataka, takra sirodhara
etc can be advocated.
Preferable & Restricted Diet and lifestyle : Patients should be advised to follow Pathya &
restrict Apathya as mentioned in Table no:8

CASE DEFINITION
Urticaria (hives) is characterized by the rapid onset of lesions known as wheals that consist of
a central mid dermal swelling with or without surrounding erythema, with associated pruritus,
lasting anywhere from 1 to 24 hours. The term urticaria is named after the stinging nettle
plant (Urtica dioica), which contains histaminic acid. Associated angioedema can sometimes
be seen, characterized by swelling of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue lasting up
to 72 hours. 1,2
Sheetapitta is a clinical condition characterized by the presence of elevated patches in the
skin resembling that produced by the sting of the wasp (Varaṭīdaṣṭasaṁsthāna sotha), and is
associated with itching (Kandu), pricking pain (Todabahulah) vomiting (Chhardi), fever (Jvara)
and burning sensation(Daha). The term Udarda is also used to denote a similar condition. In
Sheetapitta, Vata is more predominant while Udarda is a kapha dominant condition. Elevated
reddish, itchy, round patches in the skin appearing in Sisira ritu, due to kapha dosha kopa is
called Udarda.3
INTRODUCTION3-6(Incidence/ Prevalence, Morbidity/ Mortality/ Risk Factors)
Urticaria is a common skin disease. About 8–20% of individuals in the community experience
an attack of urticaria at least once in their lifetime. 4
It can be seen in all ages and sexes but is slightly more common in young adults. In 40–50% of
the patients, urticaria and angioedema are seen in combination, only urticaria or angioedema
is seen in 40% and 20% of the people, respectively.5
Urticaria is a mast cell–driven disorder characterized by the recurrent development of hives
(urticaria) and/or swelling (angioedema).4
Urticaria affects nearly 1% of the world population, with over 100 million new cases each
year.India lacks specific epidemiological studies but contributes heavily to total global burden.
Chronic cases appear commonly in adults, especially women. India bears a significant burden
of urticaria in absolute terms—accruing the highest number of Disability-Adjusted Life Year
(DALYs) globally.
In children (<14 years) at a tertiary hospital in Northern India, 57% had spontaneous urticaria;
about 12% had dermographism, 2% had cold-induced, 1.3% aquagenic, and 1.7% cholinergic
urticaria.6,7

ETIOPATHOGENESIS
The underlying event leading to urticaria is mast cell degranulation, with release of histamine
and other proinflammatory molecules. There are numerous stimuli that can lead to mast cell
activation through various pathways (Fig.1).
Fig1: Diagrammatic Overview of Urticaria
This release can be triggered by allergic, pseudoallergic, toxic, and physical mechanisms 1
• Urticaria is allergic when specific antigens crosslink specific IgE antibodies attached to
mast cells.
• Pseudoallergic urticaria describes the release of mast cell mediators after exposure to
foods or medications but without the presence of specific immunoglobulin (IgE) antibodies.
• Endogenous or exogenous substances such as opiates, codeine, or complement proteins
can alter the sensitivity of mast cells to both the stimuli.
1. Acute urticaria
The most common cause of acute urticaria is viral infections, particularly of the upper
respiratory tract. Other common causes of acute urticaria are listed in the box below. Food-
induced type I hypersensitivity reactions are a rare cause of acute urticaria in adults, but occur
more commonly in children.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION10-14
• Lesion morphology: Wheals are abrupt, well-circumscribed, raised, itchy erythematous
to pale lesions varying from millimeters to several centimeters; they appear, migrate, and
typically resolve within twenty-four hours without residual marks. They cause intense
pruritus and/or burning sensations.
• Angioedema: Characterized by sudden swelling of deeper dermis, subcutaneous tissue, or
mucosa (e.g., lips, eyes, genitals); often painful (not pruritic), resolving within up to 72 hours
• Distribution & duration: Can affect any part of body, including scalp, palms, and soles.
• Associated symptoms: May include systemic manifestations like headache, dizziness,
throat tightness, wheezing, GI discomfort (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), arthralgia, fever etc.
• Dermographism & physical triggers: Stroking skin may reproduce wheals
(“dermatographism”) within minutes; characteristic of physical urticaria-physical factors
(pressure, temperature changes, vibration, sunlight) may precipitate symptoms
• Alarming features indicating vasculitis or anaphylaxis: Wheals lasting more than 24
hours, painful, non-blanching, or leaving purpura/hyperpigmentation suggest urticarial
vasculitis. Associated symptoms such as hypotension, stridor, GI symptoms, or confusion
point toward systemic anaphylaxis.

Differential Diagnosis in Ayurveda
Differential diagnosis of Sheetapitta should be made from Udarda, Kotha/Utkotha, Visarpa
and Kotham -Kustha.
Sheetapitta is associated with picking pain and itching, aggravated at evening time. The
differentiation is given as:
• Udarda: considered a Tridoshaja Vyadhi, Kapha produces kandu, Vata induces toda and
Chardi and jvara by Pitta with Kapha predominance, distinguishing it from Sheetapitta,
which has Vata-Pitta dominance. Skin eruptions look alike, but Kapha dosha is predominant
; Udarda is usually aggravated at morning and sometimes it looks like skin colour.
• Kotha/Utkotha: features like itching and swelling are more prominent. In Kotha eruptions
are numerous in number and small in size 24
• Visarpa: Rapidly spreading skin lesions, often with systemic symptoms.25
• Kotham-Kustha: not an acute condition- discoloration, scaling, oozing, and localized
skin disease; Sheetapitta is more acute and episodic. Kotham (Kustha/skin disease, often
psoriasis or eczema-like) is considered a Kapha–Pitta dominant disorder with deeper tissue
involvement.26

SUPPORTIVE INVESTIGATIONS27-34
Some principles that determine the investigation are:
1. Acute urticaria is generally not investigated.
2. Acute recurrent urticaria is frequently clarified with a history, as a possible trigger (food,
medication, activity) can be identified. One should not forget to enquire about mucosal
contacts, such as toothpaste, latex condoms, or even semen. Everything that comes in
contact with the mucosa should be sought for, like drugs (prescription and over-the-
counter; ask directly about aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]),
all foodstuffs including spices, drinks and even chewing gum.
3. Chronic urticaria often remains idiopathic. Now there is a concept of endotypes and there
are certain investigations that can be employed to differentiate the types of CSU, but they
relate to the course and preferred treatment and need expert interpretation by centres
that are proficient in these tests. Certain drugs like anti histamines, Omalizumab and BTK
inhibitors are prescribed on the basis of these tests and endotype classification.

DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA
The diagnosis will be done based upon the clinical presentation, clinical examination and
investigations as mentioned above.
• Ayurvedic Diagnostic Approach:
• Nidana (Etiological Factors): Includes exposure to cold breeze, incompatible foods
(Viruddha Ahara), and seasonal triggers.
• Dosha Assessment: Predominant involvement of Vata and Pitta with Rakta and Rasa as
affected dhatus.
• Twak Vikara Evaluation: Observation of skin lesions, itching (Kandu), burning sensation
(Daha), and swelling (Shotha).
• Rogabala and Vyadhibala: Strength of the disease and the patient’s immunity are
considered for treatment planning.
PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT
The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating
treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated co
morbidities. If the patient is already under standard care, the physician may advice to continue
the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can be assessed for the same in the
follow ups for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional
physician.
Red Flag Signs
These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment for need for management/
consultation through modern medicine.
• Angioedema of airway structures & family History.
• Respiratory distress (stridor, wheezing).
Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders 101

• Cardiovascular signs (hypotension, tachycardia, syncope).
• Hives that persist > 24–48 hours or ulcerate.
• Systemic signs (fever, weight loss, night sweats, arthralgia).Chronic hives (> 6 weeks).
• Urticaria as a part of severe allergic reaction.
• Urticaria with symptoms of anaphylaxis (dizziness, breathing troubles and swelling of
tongue, lips, mouth or throat).
(A) Prevention Management35,36
 Hydration: Maintain adequate water intake to support skin hydration and overall health.
 Avoid known triggers. (Nidana Parivarjan)
 Regular moderate exercise: Promotes immune balance.
 Sleep and environmental controls: Ensure proper sleep hygiene; maintain cool, well-
ventilated surroundings; choose breathable, loose cotton clothing.
 Bath and change of clothes: If pollen or animal contact has triggered urticaria in the past,
take a bath and change clothes.
Yoga37
Regular practice of yogic techniques such as Neti (nasal cleansing), selected Asanas—
including Tadasana (Palm Tree Pose), Trikonasana (Triangle Pose), Veerabhadrasana I & II
(Warrior Poses I & II), Setu Bandhasana (Bridge Pose), and Shavasana (Corpse Pose)—along
with breathing practices (Pranayama) such as Nadi Shodhana (alternate nostril breathing),
Bhramari (humming bee breathing), and Sheetali (cooling breath), play a significant role in
maintaining overall health.
These practices collectively help in reducing psychological stress, improving blood circulation,
facilitating detoxification, and regulating immune function. Furthermore, the inclusion of
Dhyana (meditation) and Yoga Nidra (yogic relaxation) enhances mental stability and promotes
psychosomatic balance. Together, these interventions contribute to strengthening the body’s
natural defense mechanisms and may aid in reducing the risk or progression of disorders such
as Urticaria.

Line of treatment:
The treatment of Sheetapitta is based on the doshagati 38 and includes Shamana, shodhana,
and Bahi Parimarjana Chikitsa. 39 Krimighna and Dadrughna drugs can also be added subject
to involvement of dosha40and the line of treatment is similar to that of Kushtha, Amlapitta and
Udarda.41

FollowUp: In the first-level management of Sheetapitta, which primarily involves Nidana
Parivarjana (avoiding causative factors), intake of shamanoushadhis and dietary regulation, the
follow-up period is relatively short and focused on early symptom resolution and prevention
of escalation.
Initial Phase (Days 1–7)
• Frequency: Every 3–5 days
• Purpose: Monitor response to initial interventions
• Focus: Reduction in itching (Kandu), swelling (Shotha), and redness (Raga)
Stabilization Phase (Weeks 2–4)
• Frequency: Weekly
• Purpose: Ensure sustained relief and prevent recurrence
• Focus: Evaluate digestion (Agni), skin condition, and adherence to Pathya-Apathya
guidelines
Transition Criteria to Second-Level
If symptoms persist beyond 2–3 weeks or recur after initial relief or new symptoms like Daha,
Jwara, or Chhardi appears, the patient may be referred to level 2.
Referral Criteria
• If symptoms cannot be controlled with regular treatment and even after avoidance of
triggering factors.
• Patients suffering from angioedema.
• Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living.
• Evidence of an increase in severity/complications
• Diagnostic uncertainty.
• Uncontrolled comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension etc.

• Urticaria with symptoms of anaphylaxis.
• Hereditary angioedema, physical urticaria not responding to treatment.
AT LEVEL 2: (CHC/Small hospitals (10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such as
routine investigations, X-ray)
Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Level 1
Non-responding cases of mild to moderate severity and severe cases shall be referred to
level 2 and 3. The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be evaluated thoroughly
for any complications.Identification of patient specific etiopathological factors (nidana), dosha
involvement (Initial kapha-vata dominance may start showing signs of Pitta aggravation) and
assessment of Rogibala is needed before initiation of treatment.
Investigations: The diagnosis would be primarily clinical. Investigations may be necessary (if
not done at primary level) to investigate complications or exclude other differential diagnoses
as follows:
• Infection screens
• Thyroid Panels
Management
The second level management of Sheetapitta includes Shamana as well as Shodhana
Chikitsa—a purificatory approach used when symptoms are chronic, recurrent, or associated
with Bahudosha Avastha (excessive doshic aggravation).
Purification/other procedures
1. Vamana (Therapeutic Emesis)
• Decoctions of Patola, Nimba, Vaca used for emesis
• Eliminates Kapha and Ama from the Amasaya
• Indicated when itching and swelling are predominant
2. Virechana (Purgation Therapy)
• Triphala Churna, Trivrit Avaleha, Navakarshika Kashaya
• Targets Pitta and Rakta Dushti
• Especially useful when burning sensation (Daha) and redness (Raga) are prominent
Recommended Follow-Up Period
Immediate Post-Shodhana Phase (Days 1–7)
• Frequency: Daily or alternate days
• Focus: Monitor Samyak Lakshana (signs of proper purification), bowel movements,
hydration, and vitals
• Care: Begin Samsarjana Krama (gradual diet restoration) with Manda, Peya, Vilepi
Recovery Phase (Weeks 2–4)
• Frequency: Weekly
• Focus: Assess reduction in symptoms like Kandu, Daha, Shotha
• Care: Introduce Shamana Chikitsa if needed, continue dietary regulation

Maintenance Phase (Weeks 5–12)
• Frequency: Biweekly to monthly
• Focus: Prevent recurrence, monitor Agni, Bala, and skin health
• Care: Use Rasayana therapy (e.g. Haridrakhand, Guduchi, Triphala) to rebuild immunity
Referral Criteria
• Same as mentioned earlier at Level 1
• Failure to respond to initial medical management/ Acute exacerbation of the disease
• Hereditary angioedema
• Physical urticaria not responding to therapy
• Any other life-threatening complications
• Clinical diagnosis referral from second-level to third-level is considered when symptoms
intensify or become chronic, requiring deeper detoxification.
AT LEVEL 3: (Ayush hospitals attached with teaching Institution, DistrictLevel/ Integrated/
State Ayush Hospitals)
Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Levels 1 & 2.
Confirm diagnosis and severity with the help of following investigations.
• Screening for neutrophil rich infiltrates in skin biopsy, performing gene mutation analysis
for hereditary periodic fever syndromes.
• Autologous Serum Skin Test (ASST)
• In cases of suspected hereditary angioedema (HAE), test for complement C4 levels, If mean
wheal duration >24 hours, perform biopsy of skin lesion to assess for signs of urticarial
vasculitis.
• Complement activity tests.
• Anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and/or anti-citrullinated protein.
• Thyroid autoantibodies to TSH receptor, thyroglobulin, thyroid peroxidase and sodium/
iodine symporter.
• Biopsy to be done when there is doubt regarding the diagnosis (lesions persisting beyond
24 hrs, non-blanchable, fever, joint pains etc.)
• This level is applied when the disease is chronic or relapsing and there is significant doshic
involvement (especially Pitta and Rakta)
Management

sodhana therapies.

CASE DEFINITION:1, 2, 3, 4
Vitiligo is a chronic, acquired autoimmune skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated
hypopigmented or depigmented macules and patches resulting from the selective destruction
of melanocytes in the epidermis. It may affect the skin, mucous membranes, and hair follicles,
and can be associated with systemic autoimmune conditions such as thyroiditis, uveitis, and
sensorineural hearing loss.
Before adressing vitiligo, it is important to understand the basic target cell that is affected
by the disease and for that a basic overview of the melanin pathway is essential. Melanin is
formed from the essential amino acids tyrosine and phenylalanine through a series of enzymatic
steps in the liver and skin. Tyrosine is formed in the liver by the hydroxylation of the essential
amino acid phenylalanine under the influence of phenylalanine hydroxylase which is in turn
converted to DOPA and further into the pigment under the influence of tyrosinase enzyme (Fig.
1). The melanin is made within the melanosomes which are of two types —eumelanosomes
(containing eumelanin), or pheomelanosomes (containing pheomelanin). These melanosomes
pass into the dendritic processes of the melanocyte to be further transferred into neighboring
keratinocytes.

Case Definition in Ayurveda:
Shvitra is characterized by whitish, de-pigmented areas without exudation and non-infectious
patches on the skin (अपटरस्ाविवितेतिणचिमं्डला)5. The term Shvitra is a combination of Shweta and
Rak.
Shweta means whiteness, and Rak is a suffix of ‘Shweta’Dhātu.TheNirukti of the term reveals
white colour or changes toward white colour.
Synonyms: Kilasa, Shweta, Shouklya, Aruna, and Daruna.
INTRODUCTION (Incidence/Prevalence, Morbidity/Mortality/Risk Factors)7, 8, 9, 10
• Vitiligo, a common depigmenting skin disorder, has an estimated prevalence of 0.5–2%
of the population worldwide. The prevalence of vitiligo is quite variable around the world,
being more frequent in Africa (0.4%), Europe (0.4%), and Oceania (1.2%), than in North
America (0.2%) and Asia (0.1%).
• In India, the reported prevalence of vitiligo ranges from approximately 0.5% to 2.5%, with
some regional studies indicating even higher figures in specific populations.
• There is no difference in prevalence between races or genders. Females typically acquire
the disease earlier than males. Onset may occur at any age, although about half of patients
will have vitiligo by 20 years of age.
• It is broadly classified into nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV) and segmental (SV), with NSV
being the most common form.
• Vitiligo significantly impacts patient’s psychological and social well-being.
In Ayurveda, nearly all skin conditions are classified generally as sub-varieties of Kustharoga
and come under the general categories of “Kustharogadhikara” while a few are also described
under “Kshudrarogadhikara”. However, among the different types of Kustha that are described
in Brihattrayi, Shvitra has not been named as a sub type. But due to the Vaisishthaya
(specificity) of the presentation, Shvitra is discussed separately in the Kustha chapter, which
gives it particular attention.11

Updates in pathogenesis and its relevance 12, 13, 14
Various theories have been propounded for the causation of vitiligo which are listed in the box
below
1. Genetic predisposition
2. Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes.
3. Neural pathways (explains the stress and segmental type)
4. Metabolic abnormalities & oxidative stress - Accumulation of toxic metabolites and oxidants that
damage melanocytes.
5. Self destruction of melanocytes (autocyto destructive)
The effect of these factors is largely confined to autoimmune damage which has a close
relationship of specific immune cells and cytokines which are important as many new drugs
have been approved to target the specific cytokines which helps to prevent “by-stander cells”
and also helps to ensure targeted therapy
The autoimmune theory revolves around the role of CD8+ T-cells and T cells. The former
RM
is a cell that causes cell damage and the latter is a memory cell that leads to relapses. In
fact, formal studies have shown that biopsies of vitiligo show melanocyte destruction with
presence of melanocyte specific CD8+T-cells as compared to controls. These T-cells result in
cell damage apoptosis via the release of IFN-γ which mediates it action via JAK/STAT pathway.
Etiological Factors:15
The etiological factors of Shvitra include the factors responsible for the causation of the
Samanya Kustha. They can be classified as
Aaharaja (Dietary factors):
• Intake of incompatible food combinations (Virudha Ahara) such as milk with fish
• Intake of unctuous and heavy-to-digest drinks (Snigdha-Guru Pana)
• Simultaneous intake of hot and cold potency foods and irregular fasting
• Overeating, eating uncooked food, or eating before previous meal is digested
• Excessive intake of freshly harvested grains, curd, fish, salt, and sour substances
• Excessive intake of black gram (Masha), radish (Mulaka), sesame (Tila), and jaggery
Viharaja (Lifestyle factors):
• Suppression of natural urges like vomiting
• Excessive physical exercise in hot weather or after a heavy meal
• Use of cold water immediately after exposure to scorching sun, exertion, or during a
frightening situation
• Sleeping during daytime
• Improper administration of Panchakarma therapies

Samprapti (Pathogenesis)
The vitiated Doshas aggravated as a result of the indulgence in regular use of aggravating
dietary and lifestyle factors and those particularly prone, as a result of specific Nidana, lead
to the Sanga (obstruction) of the Rasavaha and Raktavahasrotasa. The aggravated Doshas
vitiate the specific dhatu and result in the specific discoloration of the skin i.e. reddish, coppery
or whitish, depending upon the Dhatu involved. The classics define Tritiya Twacha (the third
layer of skin, as per Acharya Charaka) or Tamra (the fourth layer of the skin, as per Acharya
Sushruta) to be the Adhisthana (site of occurrence) of the Kilasa.16 That is why the external as
well as internal medication is required for Shvitra treatment.
CLINICAL PRESENTATION 17, 18
Vitiligo is clinically defined by the appearance of well-demarcated hypopigmented or
depigmented macules and patches, resulting from the selective loss of functional melanocytes.
These lesions are typically asymptomatic, though mild pruritus may occasionally be reported.
In individuals with darker skin tones, the contrast between affected and unaffected areas is
more pronounced. Lesion margins may exhibit intermediate hypopigmented zones, forming
characteristic patterns such as trichrome or hypochromic vitiligo. Poliosi- depigmentation of
hair within affected areas, often presenting as white locks on the scalp—is considered an
indicator of deeper melanocyte involvement. Due to the absence of melanin, depigmented
regions are more vulnerable to solar erythema. In cases of universal vitiligo, widespread
depigmentation is observed. Additionally, lesions may develop at sites of skin trauma, a
phenomenon known as koebnerization.
An international consensus in 2011 standardized the classification of vitiligo, distinguishing
segmental vitiligo (SV) from all other forms, which were grouped under non-segmental
vitiligo (NSV). The consensus also introduced mixed vitiligo—coexistence of SV and NSV
in a single patient—as a clinically distinct subgroup, categorized under NSV due to similar
pathophysiological behaviour.
