CLINICAL EXAMINATION 21, 22
Important points of history that are helpful in the diagnosis of vitiligo include:
• Age at onset of lesions
• Factors or events that may cause the onset of vitiligo
• Symptoms associated with the lesions
• Progression or spread of lesions
• Changes observed in lesions over time
• Presence of concomitant diseases
• Current medications
• Occupational history/ exposure to chemicals or radiation
• Family history of vitiligo and autoimmune diseases
Physical Examination of vitiligo will include these features:
• The most affected areas include the face, neck, forearms, dorsal hands, fingers, feet, and
scalp. On the face, lesions typically show a periocular or perioral distribution.
• In cases of generalized involvement, lesions may also be seen on the areolae, nipples, and
genital region. Sites frequently exposed to friction or trauma- such as bony prominences
(elbows, knees) are often involved, which may reflect the Koebner phenomenon, observed
in 20–60% of vitiligo cases.
• Vitiligo manifests as depigmented macules or patches with a convex border without signs
of inflammation with normal skin around.
• Macules are milky-white in color, well-demarcated with any shape
• Ranges in size from a few millimeters to a few centimeters.
• Signs of other associated diseases may also be present like goiter, anemia, generalized
wasting, premature grey hairs, alopecia areata and weakness, etc
• Leukotrichia, or depigmentation of body hair within vitiliginous macules, may be noted
during examination and is considered a marker of poor response to repigmentation
therapies, as spontaneous recovery of pigment in affected hair is uncommon.

DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA39
Vitiligo is typically diagnosed clinically, based on the presence of acquired, amelanotic,
non-scaly, chalky-white macules with well-defined margins. These lesions often follow
characteristic distribution patterns, including periorificial areas, lips, distal extremities, genitalia,
segmental zones, and sites of friction.
Confirmatory laboratory investigations are generally unnecessary, except when required to
rule out other differential diagnoses. Histopathological examination of the central portion of
a vitiligo lesion reveals complete loss of melanin pigment in the epidermis and an absence of
melanocytes. Occasionally, lymphocytic infiltration may be observed at the advancing margins
of the lesions, suggesting active disease progression.

The clinical criteria for the diagnosis of segmental vitiligo: 39
Essential criteria (major)
• Acquired depigmented macules occurring unilaterally not crossing the midline or with
minimal spill onto the opposite side
• Localized to a particular body area/site
• Patterned distribution
including recognizable patterns, viz., blaschkoid, dermatomal, phylloid, checkerboard,
linear/oblong or any other specific type
Additional criteria (minor)
• Age at onset <15 years
• Leucotrichia >50% over the affected lesion
• Leucotrichia extending beyond the margin
• Presence of islands of normal or hyperpigmentation within the lesion or segment
without treatment
• Margins >50% irregular/straight line
• Stability achieved in disease progression by 1 year
Patients fulfilling all essential and one or more of the additional criteria are classified as
segmental vitiligo and remaining patients as nonsegmental vitiligo.

PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT
The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating
treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated co
morbidities. If the patient is already under standard care, the physician may advise to continue
126 Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders

the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can be assessed for the same in the
follow ups for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional
physician.
It must be noted that the therapy should address TWO key issues
1 Repigmentation
2. Stopping the Autoimmune process
As pigment cells are only present deep in the hair follicles, treatments mostly try to get
melanocytes to divide and migrate into affected skin. The aims of vitiligo treatment are
repigmentation and stabilization of the depigmentation process. In addition, agents that help
to ameliorate the oxidative stress are a useful adjunct. The choice of therapy depends on the
extent, location, and activity of disease as well as the patient’s age, skin type and motivation
to undergo treatment. In general, a period of at least 2–3 months is required to determine
whether a particular treatment is effective. The areas of the body that typically have the best
response to medical therapy are the face, neck, midextremities and trunk, while the distal
extremities and lips are the most resistant to treatment.
Red Flag Signs
These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment.
• Rapidly spreading or widespread depigmentation – suggests active disease needing
early intervention.
• Poliosis (white hair in lesions) – Indicates deep melanocyte loss; often resistant to
treatment.
• Mucosal or genital involvement – Associated with higher psychosocial impact and poor
response.
• Onset after age 60 or in infants – Atypical; consider alternative diagnoses (e.g.,
lymphoma, post-inflammatory changes).
• Associated autoimmune diseases – Screen for thyroid, diabetes, etc.
(A) Prevention
The prevention of vitiligo involves a three-tiered approach: Primary, Secondary, and
Tertiary prevention.
• Primary prevention aims to reduce the risk of disease onset by avoiding known
triggers such as skin trauma, chemical exposure, and excessive sunburn, while
promoting immune health through stress management, a balanced antioxidant-rich
diet, and healthy lifestyle practices.
• Secondary prevention focuses on early identification and prompt treatment to
prevent disease progression, along with sun protection and regular monitoring using
validated tools like the VIDA score.
• Tertiary prevention is directed toward managing established vitiligo, enhancing
repigmentation through individualized therapy, addressing psychosocial concerns
with counseling, improving cosmetic appearance, and monitoring for associated
autoimmune conditions.

Diet 40
Emerging evidence suggests that nutritional modulation may aid in vitiligo prevention and
management by supporting melanocyte health and reducing oxidative stress. A diet rich in
antioxidants, vitamins, and minerals is recommended.
• Recommended dietary components:
• Antioxidants (Vitamin C, E, β-carotene, selenium, zinc)
• Folic acid, Vitamin B12, and Copper (important for melanogenesis)
• Phytochemicals (from fruits, vegetables, green tea, turmeric)
Lifestyle 41
Lifestyle practices that reduce physical and psychological stress are vital, as stress is a
known trigger for vitiligo onset and progression.
• Avoidance of skin trauma (e.g., tight clothing, cosmetic irritants) to reduce Koebner
phenomenon
• Stress management techniques such as meditation, mindfulness, and counseling
• Adequate sun protection to prevent photodamage of depigmented skin
• Maintenance of sleep hygiene and regular circadian rhythms
Yoga 42
Yoga and related practices have shown beneficial effects in vitiligo, primarily through modulation
of the immune system, stress reduction, and enhancement of systemic antioxidant status.
Some of the practices found helpful are as follows:
• Pranayama (breathing exercises)
• Surya Namaskar (sun salutation)
• Shavasana, Yoga Nidra for relaxation
• Meditation to reduce anxiety and autoimmune activation
• (Proper guidance from a yoga expert is essential before practicing yoga for skin
disorders)
B) Curative
• Shodhana (Purification therapies)
For Shodhana, generally Vamana (therapeutic emesis) and Virechana (therapeutic purgation)
are used, and Basti (medicated enema) may be administered if necessary. After achieving
proper purification (Samyak Shuddhi) and following the Samsarjana Krama (gradual dietary
regimen), the following special therapeutic procedures are advised for the treatment of
Shvitra (vitiligo). These procedures, when systematically administered, can lead to the desired
formation of therapeutic eruptions or lesions (Sphotas).

Referral Criteria
Patients with vitiligo should be referred to a higher-level facility (Level 2 or 3) under the
following circumstances:
• Uncertain Diagnosis – Atypical presentation or diagnostic confusion with other
hypopigmented disorders (e.g., leprosy, pityriasis alba, tinea versicolor).
• Rapid Progression – Sudden and extensive spread of depigmented lesions.
• Mucosal or Extensive Involvement – Vitiligo affecting genital mucosa, lips, eyelids, or
involving 10% of body surface area.
Standard Treatment Guidelines in Ayurveda on Dermatological Disorders 133

• Severe Psychological Distress – Evidence of anxiety, depression, or social withdrawal due
to cosmetic impact.
• Unresponsive to Initial Management – No improvement after a reasonable period of
individualized care.
• Suspected Associated Autoimmune Disorders – Presence of signs suggestive ofthyroid
disease, diabetes, or adrenal insufficiency requiring investigation and specialist input.
• Uncontrolled comorbidities.
• Evidence of an increase in severity/complications.
• Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living

routine, investigation, X-ray)

• Complete Haemogram

symptoms.
• Review previous treatments and response.
Categorization:

• Shamana suitable: Mild, localized, early-stage cases.

Shamana Chikitsa Protocol:

◊ Combine internal medications with local therapies (Lepa, Suryapadsantap, etc.).
◊ Simple Raktamokshana may be done if expertise is available.

Referral Criteria
Patients at Level 2 should be referred to higher centers under the following conditions:
• Same as mentioned earlier at level 1, plus
• No clinical improvement or worsening despite appropriate homoeopathic management.
• Complications requiring advanced diagnostic tools or specialty care.
• Need for multidisciplinary evaluation or emergency care.
• Non-responsiveness in suspected autoimmune, systemic, or rapidly progressing
pathology.
• Diagnostic uncertainty requires investigation beyond the available infrastructure.
• Referral should be made to Ayush Level 3 or appropriate higher-level healthcare
facilities with specialist services and comprehensive diagnostic setups.
• Any other complications that threaten the life of the patient.
Level 3- (Ayush hospitals attached with teaching Institution, District Level/Integrated/State
Ayush Hospitals)
Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Level 1 & 2.
Confirm diagnosis and severity with the help of investigations such as:
• Thyroid function tests (TSH, fT3, fT4), anti-thyroid antibodies, ANA, fasting glucose levels,
HbA1c.
• Wood’s lamp examination can be used to enhance the visibility of depigmented lesions,
particularly in fair-skinned individuals or early-stage disease. If needed, differential diagnosis
from other hypopigmented conditions (e.g., pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory
hypopigmentation) can be aided by routine investigations and clinical pattern recognition.
